About a year ago I was invited to give a lecture designed to spark critical thinking in graduate students when considering using generative AI and other tools that had started applying the “artificial intelligence” label in order to seem shiny and new. Being me, I wanted something to hang the presentation on and as I put together the topics that I wanted to address an acronym emerged. This framing has appeared to help a variety of audiences to engage with these questions and so here is a very casual description.

This is the ACToRS in AI Framework.

Context: For anyone who doesn’t know me personally: I don’t actively use generative AI tools, I openly talk about the need to reject and refuse them, and I deactivate whatever I can whenever possible. I am unimpressed by the sprint many edtech vendors are on to shove badly designed OpenAI/Anthropic/Co-Pilot/Gemini wrappers into their products, followed by breathless announcements about how they now need to charge us so much more for something that is inconsistent, wrong, or a glorified CTRL-F. It’s the new plastic or worse, the new glitter. My students are not allowed to use generative tools in my classroom and the graduate students I supervise who work on pre-submission grant materials are likewise not allowed to use them for any work they complete for me.

Unlike the race-to-adopt folks, I also have to put in the various caveats that yes, I’m aware that algorithmic work, machine learning, natural language processing, the use of neural networks, etc. has been scholarship for the better part of 50 years and has value and there are targeted projects on which they are incredible tools. I’m not talking about that, I’m talking about the desperation to shove a “summary bot” into every library database, having to bang on Microsoft Office regularly to get it to turn off Co-pilot chat yet again ( Apple users encounter this too ) ( more ways to turn things off here ), and avoiding whatever I can in Canvas that is trying to put a de-humanized layer between me and my students. As Dr. Timnit Gebru noted on Bluesky recently, we’re stuck debunking hype instead of getting to actually do the novel work we wish to engage with.

## The ACToRS Framework

The ACToRS framework is a lens in which to consider the products and vaporware that is being marketed to us, to consider what problem we are trying to solve, and to take a step back from the exclamation points and assertions of Faster! Better! Now! It stands for the following:

- Accountability

- Credit

- Trust

- Risk

- Surveillance

I typically open this lecture pointing out that while I am about to take them through a variety of things to consider, I do not have individual answers for my audience members. This framework is to encourage you to think, examine, explore, and inquire. Additionally, I will not post comments where individuals ask me to excuse them of their own culpability with using these products “because of this ONE reason.” I am not here to grant absolution.

When we’re talking about AI and these various products that are invading our screens and tools, who is held accountable? Who is actually responsible for the data or the information in a paper, a response given to a client, a patent, the code, an assignment, the health outcome, or a team project?

We’ve seen a remarkable ceding of accountability by businesses, whether we’re talking about the frontier models ( “The AI got out! We can’t be accountable for what it did!” ) or other companies just happening to have an AI outcome that is so significantly in their favor ( healthcare rejections anyone? ). There’s a pervasive use of language that rejects any responsibility for a poor outcome that catches attention.

And when accountability does trickle into things, it’s often with a traditional hierarchy in mind — people with power are excused while the intern, the junior employee, or the student is assigned the blame or the responsibility. Increasingly we are seeing retractions or misconduct hearings across the academy which authors must combat against accusations of LLM usage or plagiarism. Never mind that it was the workplace, the manager, the senior researcher, or the instructor who created and supported the environment where speed and reaching a pre-specified outcome was assigned. Accountability also comes up when we’re discussing who is responsible for a variety of mental health crises that we have seen with chatbot usage. This can lead to pseudo-relationships and other forms of harm and there are presently lawsuits from distraught families . Will the companies be held accountable?

Adjacent to or sometimes on the other hand of accountability is who gets credit when generative AI is used? This is a question that will earn many lawyers significant fees, as we navigate c opyright or trademark law. But we should start with the questions of determining who (or what) gets credit for a presentation, a publication, or a patent.

One group I have presented this framework to is graduate students in Chemistry. Many of them are very interested in working in pharmaceuticals or other industries where they might go onto have patents and the associated revenues attached to their names. Once we have considered the potential for accountability, we now must flip that — if we say that a business must be accountable for the output of an LLM or a chatbot , shouldn’t we also then give credit to a discovery generated by a chatbot? It’s not quite the equivalent but we’ve done this already with Google’s DeepMind and the Nobel Prize .

And OpenAI certainly seems to want the credit for outputs — claiming credit for solving a math problem where ChatGPT was used purportedly in private mode.

While it appears to be increasingly understood that LLM generated text isn’t copyrightable – with fiction publishers requiring attestation by authors because otherwise they cannot get an appropriate contract (yes, even though those same publishers were selling their back catalog to the frontier model companies for training). In academic publishing, journals remind authors that LLMs cannot take responsibility and therefore cannot get the credit for text in articles. Also walking the line of accountability and credit is how the NIH asserted over a year ago that applications “substantially developed by AI” were not the original ideas of the applicants and may be considered research misconduct .

A lot of my work and my background comes through and from the health sciences — an area where generative tools are supposed to take the place of clinicians, magically solve documentation issues, sort out differential diagnosis, and a host of other activities. Whether or not patients trust what is being marketed to them is continuously a question. But trust comes up in a variety of ways:

- Do we trust the image, the citation, the article, the analysis, the conclusion? Or do we believe it’s been faked? Earlier I wrote about how generative tools are creating more, not less work for me . The increase of need for verification has grown exponentially.

- Do we trust the person? I stopped writing with a junior peer because he gave me multiple articles to include in a reference list that didn’t exist. I have to determine how much I trust my students to follow my directives in class to use their own brain rather than sprint through their homework by having an LLM extrude it. I have to trust a journal peer reviewer not to put my pre-publication manuscript through frontier-model-du-jour.

- Do we trust the company? Did they toss up an LLM-generated image that we’re supposed to trust looks remotely like the product they sell, the food they serve, the apartment you’re attempting to rent?

- For my students, do you trust the professor who has clearly had a model extrude the lecture, possibly also the text for the lecture, an automated voice to do the recording…

There have been some calls for transparency to serve as a way to build trust. If you disclose what AI tools you use ( ala the call by the NY mayor for agents to disclose AI usage on images for real estate ), then consumers, readers, collaborators, etc have a better idea and can in theory make a more informed decision about whether or not they want to proceed. Transparency can, potentially, help. I’d rather have it than not, but we also know that people will lie and attempt to obfuscate their LLM usage because they know how it will be perceived by others. And isn’t it so interesting that they know they need to hide that behavior.

For one librarian’s take on transparency I suggest:

- Weaver KD. The Artificial Intelligence Disclosure (AID) Framework: An Introduction. College & Research Libraries News . 2024;85(10):407. doi: 10.5860/crln.85.10.407

## Risks

There are so many different risks to individuals looking at generative tools or at the companies or universities where those individuals work. An extremely few to consider

- What happens when someone knowingly uses a non-enterprise tool and puts proprietary data into it? Or identifiable human subject data? Or HR records? Or the extremely confidential report that only the upper administrators and C-suite saw?

- What happens when the individual is using a tool with an expectation of privacy and it turns out that they were on the wrong version of Co-Pilot (individual not enterprise)? Or they were using a private session but that doesn’t count for something like lawsuits or FOIA.

- What happens when advertisements in the frontier models need to be more targeted based on what you’re currently including in the chat?

- What happens when you ask someone else not to put the data into an LLM but they do anyway?

- We’ve already seen deskilling and credulous answer adoption, what happens as some skills continue to atrophy as we get reliant and cannot spot the bug or security leak in the code?

- There’s the risk of being expected to do even more with even less, and now potentially to use less AI but get the same new higher level of work done.

- Loss of originality in our writing. This goes beyond templating things, it’s homogenizing voices into that vaguely shiny noise that doesn’t quite actually have substance but certainly has good punctuation.

- For students, we see them lose opportunities as faculty are told to adopt AI as fast as possible and to use it instead of those pesky RAs/GAs who need both training and salary.

All of this adds a significant level of individual and institutional stressors. My CTO can tell you I *still* don’t fully accept the answers I’ve gotten about whether or not all of our Co-Pilot options that have been shoved into various parts of our Microsoft license do/do not fall under the contract that prevents the data being used elsewhere. And to some degree I don’t think he can reassure me of that because there’s not ways to fully do that.

Meanwhile, these risks require individuals to do it right all the time. Every single time. In a world with a million inputs, multiple devices, and often messy data management, that is setting everyone up for failure on a regular basis with wonderfully new added potential harms.

Do you know what Microsoft Purview is? It was presented to me as a tool that allowed my organization’s security team to see every input and result in/out of our institutional instance of Co-Pilot. Now – granted – I work at a public university and every email from my work account I write is FOIA-able, same with our Teams chats, files stored in Box, etc., so in some ways this is something new. However, it wasn’t something that has ever really been communicated to campus or to our students that we had this capability: that the place and the software was so easily there for them to review what had gone into or out of the tool as they were promoting that we should use it.
